children: The Federal Reserve faced a tougher policy challenge as private-sector borrowing accounted for a shrinking share of overall U.S. debt growth, potentially weakening the impact of higher interest rates, according to TS Lombard.

Economist Steven Blitz said slowing the economy through monetary policy would require a more aggressive contraction in private credit growth because the private sector had become less leveraged and its debt had become less sensitive to short-term rates.
Federal borrowing, meanwhile, had accelerated and remained largely unaffected by interest costs.

The shift had also changed the relationship between borrowing and inflation. Since 2012, federal debt growth had shown a stronger correlation with inflation, with a six-quarter lag, than household and nonfinancial business debt, which carried a four-quarter lag. Before 2012, private-sector debt growth had been more closely linked to inflation.

Blitz said the changing debt mix meant a traditional rate hike could be less effective. The most recent yield-curve inversion had lasted 25 months without producing a recession, compared with shorter inversions before previous downturns.
The note said higher federal borrowing and reduced private-sector sensitivity to rates could have made the inverted curve less effective as a tool for slowing the economy.
Instead, Blitz said Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may have considered allowing the yield curve to steepen.
Under that approach, the Fed would hold the funds rate while allowing the short end to remain cheaper and letting 10-year yields rise to reflect supply and demand for capital.

For now, Blitz said he expects Warsh to find a way through the CPI data and avert a September hike, allowing the curve to steepen instead. If the Fed did hike, the note said the usual trade of buying 30-year Treasurys and selling 10-year notes might not work this time.

title: Warsh’s rate hike puzzle: Why the old Fed playbook may fail
